Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
710 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* No significant changes from previous forecast thinking

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 215 PM Thursday...

1) Hot temperatures to persist through the end of the week, with 
limited cooling this weekend. Warm temperature return next week. 

2) Unsettled weather returns Friday and Saturday with a Marginal 
Risk for excessive rain (flash flooding). 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 157 PM Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Hot temperatures to persist through the end of the 
week, with limited cooling this weekend. Warm temperature return 
next week. 

Early afternoon water vapor imagery reveals an upper ridge 
positioned off the SC coast, with a similarly strong (594dm) ridge 
over the Southwest US. In between, a weak longwave trough stretched 
from MI to MO which was slowly dragging a surface cold front into 
the Ohio Valley. Ahead of this front across NC, temperatures have 
warmed and dewpoints have risen quite a bit with heat index values 
approaching the triple digits in many locations south and east of 
the Triangle.

The front will be slow to approach the area, keeping NC within the 
pre-frontal warm sector through Friday. As such, increased heat 
index values near or slightly above 100 degrees will be common 
through tomorrow, with the highest values across the Triangle and 
points southeast. Deep BL mixing Friday afternoon will allow 
dewpoints to retreat slightly into the lower 70s which should keep 
obs several degrees below Heat Advisory criteria, although those who 
are sensitive to the heat should take the proper precautions through 
the end of the week.

As the front approaches the area on Saturday, it'll wash out and/or 
retreat back northward early next week. Cloud cover will keep 
temperatures in check with highs Saturday and Sunday in the 
mid/upper 80s. The front will result in slightly lower thicknesses 
and dewpoints across NC next week, but still with highs in the upper 
80s to lower 90s. Dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s should keep heat 
index values in the low to mid 90s. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Unsettled weather returns Friday and Saturday with 
a Marginal Risk for excessive rain (flash flooding). 

As mentioned above, a slow moving cold front will approach from the 
west on Friday before stalling out, then washing out, Saturday into 
Sunday. Pre-frontal moisture advection will promote dewpoints in the 
low to mid 70s Friday and Saturday and there should be enough 
instability to support scattered shower and thunderstorm 
development. The best jet dynamics will be displaced well to our 
north and with the decaying nature of the surface boundary, 
organized severe convection looks to be limited in nature. The 
increase in moisture and relatively slow moving nature of any storms 
that develop will support an isolated risk of flash flooding, and 
nearly all of central NC remains within a WPC Marginal Risk of 
excessive rainfall. A few HREF LPMM bullseyes of more than 2" are 
present across the Coastal Plain Friday afternoon, although I would 
anticipate more areal coverage and localized heavy precip potential 
on Saturday given the nearby proximity of the decaying surface 
boundary. By Sunday the front should be non-existent with convection 
becoming more isolated and less organized.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/... 
As of 710 PM Thursday...

Most of central NC will remain VFR through the 24 hour TAF period. 
Late overnight into early Friday morning there could be a brief 
period of restrictions as it looks like an area of low stratus/fog 
could develop in the southern Coastal Plain and Sandhills. 
Confidence is low in this happening thus only a TEMPO at KRWI and 
KFAY were added. While there is a low chance of isolated to 
scattered showers/thunderstorms across the region Friday evening, 
confidence was not high enough at this time to add any mention with 
this 00Z TAF package. 

Outlook: Shower and thunderstorm chances are possible each 
afternoon/evening through the weekend, with the best chance for 
widespread rain Saturday. Additionally, low stratus and/or fog may 
develop and cause sub-VFR restrictions the next several mornings.

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...Leins
AVIATION...Helock/CA

FXUS62 KILM 102338
AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
730 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Aviation section updated.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Shower and thunderstorm chances will increase this weekend.

2) Heat and humidity will build and heat indices should exceed 
100 degrees through Monday.

3) Grand Strand minor coastal flooding is possible during 
multiple high tides over the coming days.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Shower and thunderstorm chances will increase 
this weekend.

Models look broadly similar to yesterday showing the persistent
mid and upper level ridge across the Southeast U.S. breaking
down this weekend as a shortwave digs into the mid-Mississippi
Valley region. This will remove the subsidence inversion that's
been capping us for days, and establish a deeper flow of Gulf
moisture that should bring precipitable water value up toward
2.2 inches by Saturday.

Today's isolated showers are being vertically inhibited by warm,
dry conditions aloft within the upper ridge. Once that factor 
is removed this weekend, forecast rain chances blossom: 20-40 
percent Friday, 60-80 percent on Saturday, and 50-60 percent on 
Sunday. 

None of these days appear to be washouts and model storm-total 
QPF through Sunday appears to have decreased in spots from 
yesterday. A few lucky locations should still pick up 2-3 inch 
totals over the coming days, with half inch totals likely more 
common. Storm mode should remain single-cell with 0-6 km bulk 
shear 10 knots or less. Loose storm organization along outflow 
boundaries and the seabreeze front should occur.

Storm coverage should begin to decline Monday as the 700-500 mb
ridge redevelops just to our west, intercepting the flow of Gulf
moisture. The subsidence inversion reappears in forecast
soundings by Tuesday which should lead to much drier conditions
Tuesday and Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Heat and humidity will build and heat indices should 
exceed 100 degrees through Monday.

Light south to southwest low level winds should advect plenty 
of Atlantic and Gulf moisture across the Carolinas through the 
weekend. Dewpoints remaining in the 70s coupled with well-above 
normal high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s should equal
heat indices rising above 100 degrees each day through Monday. 

Tomorrow (Friday) appears to be the hottest day of the period. 
Forecast 850 mb temps near +19C are 4C above normal and 1.5C 
above the 90th climatological percentile at the KMHX upper air 
site. Our current forecast high for Friday is still 4-5 degrees
F below daily records.

This unseasonably hot airmass should remain across the area
through Monday, but will be tempered by additional clouds and 
precipitation. By Tuesday, Canadian high pressure moving across 
New England should introduce a northeasterly low level flow 
which should bring a slightly cooler marine airmass onshore with
forecast highs generally in the 85-90 degree range Tuesday and 
Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Minor Grand Strand coastal flooding is possible 
during multiple high tides over the coming days.

September's New Moon occurs today which is leading to a period
of larger astronomical tides. Tidal anomalies along the Grand
Strand beaches as measured at Myrtle Beach's Springmaid Pier
should average around +1.0 feet today through the weekend. Half
to two-thirds of this anomaly is likely due to sea level rise 
leaving onshore winds responsible for the remainder. 

Forecast water levels should exceed flood stage at Springmaid
Pier by about 0.3 feet this evening, and may reach or slightly
exceed flood stage during high tides Friday morning through 
Sunday morning. See the recently-issued Coastal Flood Advisory 
for details.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
VFR generally expected through most of the period. Should fog 
develop tonight it will be shallow and is not forecast to lead to 
vsby restrictions. Showers and storms develop Friday but will be of 
low enough coverage to be relegated to PROB30s and tend to not 
advect north and east enough to affect ILM.

Extended Outlook... Although VFR conditions will prevail, there
is increasing potential for pop-up showers and thunderstorms
bringing brief MVFR/IFR conditions, especially Saturday and
Sunday. There is also a low potential for late night/early
morning stratus or ground fog, particularly affecting KLBT and
KFLO Saturday and Sunday.

&&

.MARINE...
Tonight through Tuesday...High pressure off the Southeast coast
is weakening as a cold front moves southward. This front is
still expected to stall across interior North Carolina Friday
night before lifting back to the north Saturday. South to
southwesterly winds should continue with speeds less than 15
knots. 

Increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms is expected
beginning late Friday night as Gulf moisture increases across 
the area, and as high pressure aloft dissipates and is replaced 
by cyclonic flow ahead of an upper level trough to our west.
Rather high chances for showers and storms should continue until
Monday when high pressure should begin to redevelop aloft.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 9 PM this evening to midnight EDT 
     tonight for NCZ107.
SC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 7 PM to 10 PM EDT this evening for 
     SCZ054-056.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...TRA
AVIATION...MBB

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
735 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Moderate Rip Current Risk all Local Beaches Today and Friday.
Elevated Risk Returns Early Next Week

- Daily Heat Index up to 107 through Sunday

- Daily Afternoon & Evening Thunderstorms. Main Hazards: Locally
Heavy Rain, Lightning & Gusty Winds Up to 40-50 mph

&&

.NEAR TERM /UNTIL 6 AM FRIDAY MORNING/...
Main Highlights through Tonight:

- Strong Storms and Localized Flooding Possible through Early this 
Evening, Mainly at Inland Locations.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk at All Area Beaches.

Afternoon surface analysis depicts Atlantic high pressure (1022 
millibars) centered near Bermuda and extending its axis 
southwestward across our area. Meanwhile, a cold front extends from 
New England through the Ohio Valley and the Mid-Mississippi Valley. 
Aloft...deep-layered ridging was positioned along the southeastern 
seaboard, with troughing progressing eastward across the Great Lakes 
and Mid-Mississippi Valleys. Otherwise, troughing was developing 
over central and western portions of the Gulf, or along the western 
periphery of the Atlantic ridge axis. Latest GOES-East derived Total 
Precipitable Water imagery indicates that deep tropical moisture 
remains in place for locations along and south of I-10, where PWATs 
were in the 2.1 - 2.4 inch range, while values north of I-10 were 
generally in the 1.9 - 2.1 inch range. High moisture levels and low 
level flow veering to a more south or south-southwesterly direction 
since yesterday have fostered scattered to numerous showers and a 
few embedded thunderstorms along the I-95 corridor early this 
afternoon, with activity mostly isolated thus far over the Suwannee 
Valley and the I-10 corridor, as well as along the U.S. Highway 301 
corridor in southeast GA. Temperatures at 19Z have climbed to the 
upper 80s and lower 90s outside of areas impacted by convection, 
with dewpoints in the 70s at inland locations and closer to 80 at 
coastal locations.

Gradually cooling temperatures aloft and the presence of deep 
tropical moisture should allow for convection to increase in 
coverage and intensity as the afternoon progresses. Convective 
outflows should merge at inland locations during the mid to late 
afternoon hours, especially for locations between the I-75 and I-95 
corridors in northeast and north central FL, with outflows then 
progressing northward and increasing thunderstorm coverage and 
intensity over the Okefenokee Swamp in interior southeast GA late 
this afternoon through the evening hours. Mesoscale boundary 
collisions should allow for convection to "pulse" and become briefly 
strong at inland locations, with stronger storms capable of 
producing downburst winds of 40-55 mph, along with frequent 
lightning strikes and torrential downpours, with localized flooding 
possible due to relatively slow storm motion. Low level flow veering 
to southwesterly this evening could bring at least scattered 
convection back towards the I-95 corridor this evening, with 
activity weakening by the mid-evening hours tonight. 

Debris cloud cover will tend to thin out after midnight, with 
southwesterly flow potentially developing some predawn convection 
along the FL Big Bend and Nature Coasts, but activity is not 
expected to cross the Suwannee River before sunrise. Fog and low 
stratus ceilings could develop over portions of interior southeast 
GA. Low level southwesterly flow will keep lows in the 70s area-
wide.

&&

.SHORT TERM /6 AM FRIDAY MORNING THROUGH SATURDAY NIGHT/...
Main Highlights This Period:

- Daily potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and localized 
flooding.

The local area remains located on the western periphery of surface 
high pressure over the Atlantic with weak high pressure aloft 
through the weekend. Southwesterly to southerly low level winds will 
remain in place, and will continue to pump deep moisture (PWATs 2-
2.3") into the area. With ample moisture in place, the weak 
subsidence associated with the mid/upper ridging will not be strong 
enough to suppress convection. Expect scattered to numerous showers 
and thunderstorms to develop each day, mainly during the afternoon 
and evening hours. The steering flow will allow for the Gulf breeze 
to move well inland each afternoon, with mergers with the Atlantic 
sea breeze occurring between the US-301 corridor towards the I-95 
corridor. With the elevated moisture aloft, showers and storms that 
do develop could bring periods of heavy rainfall and localized 
flooding. Isolated strong storms, maybe a few severe storms, could 
bring gusty winds in the 30 to 50 mph range along boundary mergers.  

Daytime highs will be in the low-mid 90s along inland locations on 
Friday and Saturday with highs in the upper 80s to around 90 along 
the coast. Overnight Lows will be in the lower to mid 70s. Heat 
index values will hover just under Heat Advisory criteria, with 
values in the upper 90s to around 107F.

&&

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Main Highlights This Period Saturday through Wednesday: 

- Daily Thunderstorms Potential Each Day Next Week

- Elevated Rip Current Risk Next Week 

By Monday, the high pressure axis will shift north resulting in a 
return to an onshore flow regime which will persist through the work 
week. Deep moisture remain in place with PWAT values above 2 inches 
persisting through at least Tuesday. This will continue to result in 
scattered to numerous showers and storms each day with localized 
flooding concerns and some potential for strong thunderstorms along 
boundary collisions. As we move into the middle to latter part of 
the work week, PWAT values will fall to seasonable around 1.75 
inches. In response, expect rain chances to fall slightly with 
coverage becoming more scattered Wednesday and Thursday. 

The onshore flow will also cause afternoon temperatures to cool 
slightly, generally topping out in the 85-90 degree range most 
places by Tuesday and Wednesday. Lows in the 70s will persist.

Rip current risk will also become elevated rather than moderate as a 
result of the pattern shift.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z FRIDAY THROUGH 00Z SATURDAY/...
Line of storms between GNV/VQQ at the start of the TAF period will 
fade this evening and bring mainly just mid/high clouds with -SHRA 
at the remaining terminals through 02-03Z time frame. VFR through 
the overnight hours at coastal terminals with light winds, while 
near calm winds at VQQ/GNV will lead to potential for LIFR CIGS and 
IFR VSBYS from 08-12Z and have continued the trend with this TAF 
package. Another active day of scattered to numerous showers and 
embedded storms at all terminals on Friday afternoon and for now 
have placed PROB30 groups for MVFR TSRA activity from 16-22Z at GNV 
and 17-23Z at VQQ/CRG/JAX/SGJ and 18-24Z at SSI. SE winds will 
develop behind sea breeze at CRG/SSI/SGJ after 16-18Z.

&&

.MARINE...


Showers and thunderstorms will continue to impact mainly the near 
shore coastal waters through the early evening hours tonight. 
Otherwise, Atlantic high pressure centered near Bermuda this 
afternoon will shift southward while gradually weakening on Friday 
as a frontal boundary shifts towards the southeastern states. This 
front will stall and weaken well to the north of our local waters 
this weekend. Prevailing winds will become southwesterly from Friday 
through the upcoming weekend, with the afternoon sea breeze shifting 
winds to southeasterly each afternoon across the near shore waters. 
Showers and thunderstorms developing over coastal locations during 
the afternoon hours will shift eastward across our local waters 
during the late afternoon and evening hours from Friday through the 
upcoming weekend. High pressure will then build down the 
southeastern seaboard early next week, with onshore winds forecast 
to develop by Monday afternoon, with breezy conditions and building 
seas forecast towards Tuesday and Wednesday of next week.

Rip Currents: Diminished winds and dropping surf will tend to lower 
the rip current risk toward the moderate range today. Prevailing 
winds will become south-southwesterly by Friday, with a lingering 
easterly ocean swell and onshore winds developing during the 
afternoon hours behind the inland moving sea breeze keeping a lower-
end moderate risk at area beaches.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

Winds will steadily veer to become southerly to southwesterly Today. 
This will allow for the Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes to 
push inland by the afternoon hours, with showers and storms 
developing and increasing in coverage near Highway 301. As weaker 
transport winds develop, dispersions will be Fair over the next few 
days. Otherwise, RH values will sit at Good levels through the 
weekend as moisture moves in from the Gulf and towards southeast 
Georgia and northeast Florida. 

Fog Potential: Gusty and erratic wind shifts will occur from 
thunderstorm activity. Patchy fog is expected across inland areas 
the next couple of mornings, with widespread dense fog unlikely.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...
As far as coastal water levels, we expect tidal water levels to peak 
to near the Action stage through Friday due to the recent onshore 
flow but mainly due to the new moon phase which is Friday, Sept 
11th. Mostly nuisance type flooding is expected for a brief time 
into the weekend, including in the St Johns River Basin.

As far as rainfall today, isolated pockets of about 4 inches are 
possible mainly across an area from eastern Marion county northward 
to around Baker county. These storms may cause temporary flooding, 
especially in any poor drainage or urbanized areas.

&&

.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  73  92  72  92 /  50  40  30  50 
SSI  77  89  77  90 /  30  40  20  50 
JAX  74  92  74  92 /  40  60  20  70 
SGJ  75  90  75  90 /  30  60  30  70 
GNV  73  92  73  91 /  70  60  30  70 
OCF  73  92  73  92 /  50  60  30  70 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

FXUS65 KBOU 101947
AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
147 PM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Mainly dry through Friday with warmer temperatures.

- Return to more unsettled pattern this weekend with a chance of
  thunderstorms especially on Sunday. Cooler Saturday, then warmer
  on Sunday.

- Unsettled pattern to persist through the week, with multiple
  cold fronts expected to bring a few more noticeable cooldowns.
  

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Thursday/...
Issued at 1203 PM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

Another quiet day is on tap for today as a dry airmass resides over 
Colorado. Latest satellite and surface observations show that mostly 
clear skies are allowing for efficient warming, with temperatures 
across the plains already above 80 degrees, mid to upper 60s for 
the higher elevations. Afternoon highs are expected to warm into 
the mid to upper 80s across the plains, with a few locations 
potentially reaching 90. The higher elevations are expected to be 
about ten degrees cooler, with mid to upper 70s to low 80s 
expected. A line of cumulus clouds resides along a convergence 
zone stretching from the eastern Palmer Divide into the Nebraska 
panhandle where the greatest surface moisture is in place. SPC 
mesoanalysis shows MLCAPE values approaching 500 J/kg along and 
east of the boundary today. Given some noticeable vertical growth 
on the latest satellite imagery, limited PoPs have been maintained
this afternoon, as any convective development would most likely 
occur along this boundary. 

Not much has changed in the short term forecast today. Friday 
is still expected to be another warm and mostly dry day across 
the forecast area. A little increase in mid-level moisture 
still looks to move into the higher elevations. We could see a 
few high-based showers in our northern mountains in the 
afternoon, but instability remains limited. CAMs show potential 
for some high-based virga showers to move across the plains in 
the late afternoon, but this would likely just lead to some gusty 
outflows and nothing more than a trace of precipitation. Between a
few degrees of warming at the 700 mb level and downsloping winds,
afternoon highs are forecast to warm into the 90s across the 
plains ahead of a cold front Friday night. A few late night 
showers will be possible with the cold front, mainly for the 
northern mountains and foothills. 

A brief cooldown is expected on Saturday behind the cold front.
Ensembles are in agreement that we will see some better moisture
return to the forecast area throughout the day as the next 
shortwave trough moves into the Pacific Northwest and starts to 
turn flow aloft more southwesterly. However, they differ fairly 
significantly on how much moisture we manage to tap into. Between 
the ECMWF and GFS ensembles, PWAT anomalies will range from 100% 
to 160% of normal Saturday afternoon. Even with the discrepancies,
between the increased moisture and better instability expected (a
few hundred Jules of MLCAPE), scattered afternoon showers/storms 
are expected to return to the higher elevations. 

Some slight changes in the long term forecast are present today 
as the NBM seems to be getting a slightly better handle on the 
arrival time of a few cooler air masses. Sunday is still on track 
to be a hot one, with afternoon highs expected to reach the mid 
90s across the plains. There is better agreement that moisture 
will increase a tad more and move into the lower elevations.
MLCAPE is expected to bump up to 600-1000 J/kg across the plains,
which could allow for some stronger storms to develop.

A more active and cooler pattern will remain in place through the
week, with multiple cold fronts expected to bring a few cooldowns
and precipitation chances. Monday is now looking to be warmer than
previously expected, with afternoon temperatures within a few 
degrees of normal ahead of a cold front that is now looking to 
arrive overnight. While there is still some time for things to 
change, it's looking like Tuesday will bring a significant 
cooldown, with afternoon highs struggling to climb out of the 60s 
for much of the lower elevations, and at least one more cold front
possible by the end of the week. 



&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Friday/...
Issued at 1129 AM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

VFR conditions will prevail for all terminals through the TAF
period. This afternoon, expect moderate ESE/SE winds to prevail
across the Denver metro. Winds will rotate clockwise towards
drainage flow beginning near 03Z (+/1 hr), with S wind speeds
increasing for KDEN and KAPA to 12-16 kts. Expect KBJC to
transition to lighter westerly flow. Tomorrow, light and variable
winds < 10 kts in the morning, particularly after 15-16Z. There
will be some mid-level moisture in place Friday afternoon, with a
very slight chance (~15%) of an isolated high-based shower and
gusty outflow after 22-23Z. With almost no instability to work 
with, confidence in such activity is low and thus not included in 
the KDEN TAF.

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$
